summary: South Korean Interim Government Activities No. 23 (Part 1), August 1947, covers mainly July-August 1947 for the US Army Military Government in Korea, compiled by the National Economic Board and the Statistical Research Division. It reports on population and refugee flows, property custody, food supply and the planned fall rice-collection regulation, prices, agriculture, coal and minerals, industrial output, foreign trade, labor, finance, transport, communications, utilities and flood repair. Part IV records the deadlocked US-USSR Joint Commission, the exchange of statements between Generals Brown, Hodge and Shtikov, Marshall's 12 August letter to Molotov, the Liberation Day ceremonies, Interim Legislative Assembly laws and the arrival of the Wedemeyer mission on 26 August. Part V covers health, education, culture and the press. Historians will find dense statistical tables, full texts of official statements, and a detailed picture of economic dependence on US civilian supply imports.
highlights: By 16 August 1947 repatriation left South Korea with 1,428,778 more arrivals than departures (2,313,966 inbound, 885,188 outbound); refugees from the North numbered 13,672 in July, about half the June figure.

National Food Regulation No. 6 of 18 August set fall 1947 rice-collection rules: committee-set farm quotas, delivery by 15 January 1948, and seizure of undelivered rice; the Assembly renamed it the Rice Collection Law.
The first official 1947 rice estimate, released 28 August, was 14,200,000 suk (2,166,920 metric tons), about 18 percent above 1946; the Seoul daily ration was cut to 2.0 hop on 7 August.

The Joint Commission stayed deadlocked over consulting Anti-Trusteeship parties; Shtikov protested leftist arrests on 20 August, Hodge denied the charges on 25 August, and Marshall asked Molotov on 12 August for a reply by 21 August.
Lt. Gen. Albert C. Wedemeyer's presidential fact-finding mission reached Seoul on 26 August, met SKIG officials on 29 August and political leaders on 30 August.
Private imports hit a record 271.7 million won in June against exports of 143.8 million; the Korean Foreign Exchange Bank opened 15 July, and Hongkong objected to the Macao trade loophole.

Bank of Chosun notes in circulation rose 1,128,779,000 won in August to 19,496,514,000; overdrafts to Military Government reached 24,191,284,000 won on 31 July; the 1947-48 budget stood at 17,908,679,200 won.
A Coast Guard vessel collided with an overloaded ferry off Tong Yong on 19 August (62 dead, 93 survivors), and 172 prisoners escaped Kongju Prison on 30 August.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover, title page, table of contents and list of 28 charts, maps and graphs for Number 1, August 1947, prepared by the National Economic Board and Statistical Research Division.

sections.title: Part I: Primary Considerations
sections.summary: Population and refugee data, including a net repatriate inflow of 1,428,778, and property custody rulings, among them that the Bank of Chosun is a Korean juridical person.

sections.title: Section 1. Population
sections.summary: Repatriation totals to 16 August, 13,672 refugees from the North in July, population shifts in Chungchong-pukto and Kyonggi-do, and data on Koreans in Japan and Manchuria.

sections.title: Section 2. Property Custody
sections.summary: Justice Department rulings on the Taiduk Agricultural Association and Bank of Chosun, emergency loans of 3,900,000 won to two textile mills, mining property sales, and bankers' questions on requisitioned dwellings.

sections.title: Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Economic section covering food collection and rationing, housing, prices, agriculture, coal and minerals, industrial output, imports and exports, and labor, with the 18 August rice regulation and a 14,200,000 suk crop estimate.

sections.title: Section 1. Food Supply
sections.summary: Grain collections of 599,744 metric tons, summer-grain quota 61.4 percent filled by 25 August, ration cut to 2.0 hop, National Food Regulation No. 6, and food imports of 513,829 tons.

sections.title: Rice Collection Regulation (National Food Regulation No. 6)
sections.summary: Full text of the 18 August regulation giving duties to governors, the Controller of Commodities and the New Korea Company, with quotas, receipts, a 15 January 1948 delivery deadline and penalties.

sections.title: Food Imports and Processed Foods
sections.summary: Korean rice trade 1926-1941, Civilian Supply foodstuff imports through 31 July, planting calendars, and flour, noodle, soy sauce, sugar and salt output and imports.

sections.title: Section 2. Housing
sections.summary: National Housing Administration (founded 16 November 1946) has no completed houses; 24,000,000 won for winter shelters for 30,000 Seoul refugees; 400 houses for dispossessed Koreans, 50 done by 30 August.

sections.title: Section 3. Prices
sections.summary: Revised controlled prices on 16 commodities from 1 August, coal prices set 2 September, rising free-market food, textile and gold prices, and weekly National Price Administration decisions.

sections.title: Section 4. Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: Rice estimate of 14,200,000 suk, cotton plan needing a 1,052,000,000 won loan, straw-bag shortage, fertilizer distribution of 153,116 tons, irrigation projects, livestock and fisheries.

sections.title: Section 5. Natural Resources
sections.summary: Coal below minimum needs, a Coal Committee formed 10 July, copper poured at Changhang on 26 July, a flash flood at Sandong tungsten mine, and timber regulation.

sections.title: Coal
sections.summary: Anthracite output near 28,000 tons a month, 53,254 tons of monthly Japanese bituminous imports, stockpiles, and railroads consuming about half of all coal.

sections.title: Minerals and Metals
sections.summary: Wartime peak output of gold, iron ore, graphite, copper, tungsten and zinc, May-July 1947 output, a 1951 forecast, Ongjin reopening and Mangdong barter of tungsten for Egyptian cotton.

sections.title: Forestry
sections.summary: Committee to regulate timber and firewood use, LSTs hauling logs from Hosan to Inchon, 1,000,000 board feet of US lumber, and inspection of vested forests such as Mitsui Norin.

sections.title: Section 6. Production and Allocations
sections.summary: Cotton shortage limiting 240,000 spindles, silk filature loans, paper, tobacco, brick and cement output, 480 vehicles for SKIG, six ships for the Coast Guard, and petroleum sales.

sections.title: Section 7. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Record June private imports of 271.7 million won, Korean Foreign Exchange Bank opened 15 July, Hongkong and Macao trade problems, Civilian Supply Program IV worth 84.7 million dollars, and UNRRA final account.

sections.title: Section 8. Labor
sections.summary: Tai Han No Chong and Chun Pyung conflict, the 29 July Kyung Sung Spinning strike, the Seoul Electric Company contract signed 13 August, and a poor factory dispensary inspection.

sections.title: Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: Finance, transport, communications, utilities and public works: 19.5 billion won notes in circulation, 628 locomotives with 372 inoperative, record July communications revenue, and flood repairs needing 477,451,000 won.

sections.title: Section 1. Finance
sections.summary: Notes in circulation 19,496,514,000 won; loan limits revised 26 August; July revenue 910,674,274 won against expenditure 2,004,096,655; budget 17,908,679,200 won; deposits of 27.9 billion won.

sections.title: Section 2. Transportation
sections.summary: Railway revenue exceeding expenditure without subsidy, 628 engines with 372 inoperative on 1 September, 10 locomotives arriving from Germany, highway tire shortage and marine bureau reorganization.

sections.title: Section 3. Communications
sections.summary: Record July revenue, staff down to 17,720, postal savings of 843,951,503 won, air mail to the US begun 8 August, and 20 post offices closed 1 August.

sections.title: Section 4. Public Utilities
sections.summary: Power from North Korea (42 million kWh in June), barge Electra assigned to Samchok, gas plants idle for lack of coal, 70 streetcars running, and approved freight and bus fare increases.

sections.title: Section 5. Public Works
sections.summary: Flood repairs needing 1,839,198 man-days and 477,451,000 won, 50,000 bags of Army cement lent, Seoul-Pusan highway slide repair, and city water projects.

sections.title: Part IV: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Liberation Day, Assembly laws, the deadlocked Joint Commission with statements by Shtikov, Brown and Hodge, Marshall's 12 August letter to Molotov, the Wedemeyer mission's 26 August arrival, and the Kongju prison escape.

sections.title: Section 1. Administration
sections.summary: General Lerch resumed command 7 August, Helmick's statement on sale of Civilian Supply goods, Central Election Committee, Liberation Day speeches, and the Wedemeyer mission arriving 26 August.

sections.title: Section 2. Interim Legislative Assembly
sections.summary: Twelve August meetings averaging 67 members, Temporary Constitution second reading 6 August, Franchise Law amendment, Rice Collection Law, temple property protection and abolition of licensed prostitution.

sections.title: Section 3. Political Activities
sections.summary: Politics revolved around the Joint Commission; the Rhee-Kim Koo merger attempt of 8 August failed; a rightist newspaper association formed 10 August; leftists objected to the Liberation Day order.

sections.title: Section 4. Interzone Activities and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: Full texts of Joint Commission statements, Marshall's 12 August letter to Molotov, the Soviet arrest protest, Hodge's reply, bi-weekly mail exchange, and 352 travel permits for Chinese nationals.

sections.title: U.S.-U.S.S.R. Joint Commission
sections.summary: Statements by Shtikov (2, 9, 14, 20, 28 August) and Brown (7, 9, 23 August) on consulting Anti-Trusteeship parties, Marshall's 12 August letter, and Soviet charges of repression.

sections.title: Interzone Activities
sections.summary: Bi-weekly mail exchanges between North and South Korea took place on 9 and 23 August.

sections.title: Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: By 23 August the Office of Foreign Affairs had issued 352 permits to Chinese nationals to travel to China on private watercraft for repatriation.

sections.title: Section 5. Justice
sections.summary: Executive Order No. 5 restricted 15 August ceremonies (548 localities, 773,000 participants); 1,596 prisoners released; 172 escaped Kongju Prison on 30 August; 19,777 inmates on 31 July.

sections.title: Section 6. Internal Security
sections.summary: Constabulary and Coast Guard in Liberation Day ceremonies, Constabulary guarding Seoul utilities, Coast Guard maneuvers on 17 August, and the 19 August Tong Yong ferry collision killing 62.

sections.title: Part V: Social
sections.summary: Health, education, culture and information media: smallpox down to 143 cases, Hangul promotion ordered 14 August, 109 missionaries, and press comment on the Joint Commission and Wedemeyer mission.

sections.title: Section 1. Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Quarantine rules strengthened 4 September, no cholera in 1947, smallpox down to 143 cases from 20,574, 60,000 UNRRA penicillin vials, and LARA shipments worth 202,000 dollars.

sections.title: Section 2. Education
sections.summary: Hangul promotion ordered 14 August, 160 Seoul National University medical students reinstated, Chosun Christian College admits women, 301 music teachers trained, and 1,010 new secondary classes.

sections.title: Section 3. Culture and Religion
sections.summary: Korean observers to the Institute of Pacific Relations conference at Stratford-on-Avon, National Youth Movement training for 55,000 men and 20,000 women, and 109 missionaries on 30 August.

sections.title: Section 4. Media of Information
sections.summary: 200 portable projectors received, newsreel No. 22, radio memorial for Lyuh Woon Hyeung, forum programs replacing political speeches, and press comment on the Joint Commission, Wedemeyer mission and trade deficit.

sections.title: Map of Korea
sections.summary: Closing page with a map of Korea from Light Area Printing Plant records, the last item in the charts and maps index.
